messages.subject: MRDS Single-observer sensitivity
parts:
Dear list,

I am revisiting an analysis that I started last year on line-transect vis=
ual=20
detection of seabirds. The data are stratified by study area (n=3D2) and =
time=20
period (n=3D3). I would like to generate 6 density estimates for each of =
the 31=20
species in the dataset, one estimate for each study-area-time-period stra=
tum.=20
Since only 10 species have > 80 detection, I estimated detection function=
s for=20
the 10 species that have obs > 60 and assigned each of the remaining 21 r=
are=20
species (obs n =3D 2-20) to a "detection group" based on their similariti=
es to=20
more abundant species (following Alldredge et al 2007).

In response to a previous post, Jeff Laake suggested that I use MRDS in t=
he=20
single-observer mode to fit a common detection function to a group of spe=
cies=20
and then get species-specific estimates within that group by running a=20=

separate analysis that filters for each species and then applies the comm=
on=20
detection function. I am following this approach and have also added=20
OBSERVER as a factor in the detection function model. I have run into two=
=20
issues with this analysis:

1. The density estimates for the most common species are 50 times higher=20=

when I apply the =93species group=94 detection function to the single spe=
cies than=20
the density estimates from the =93single-species=94 detection function. I=
n this=20
case, the single common species has 222 detections. Why does adding 33=20=

detections of rare species to the common species dataset increase the=20
density estimate so drastically?

2. The observations are binned in 50m increments and truncated at 300m. I=
s=20
the assumption that g(0)=3D1 only for distance =3D 0, or would it assume =
perfect=20
detection for the entire first bin? If so, why is the probability of dete=
ction for=20
the first bin 0.2 on the figure for the single-species model and nearly 0=
for the=20
species group?

I am struggling to understand the effects that OBSERVER and species group=
ing=20
seem to be having on the density estimates, given that the variation in=20=

estimates among models is so huge. Any advice appreciated.

Thanks,
Adrian

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: MRDS Single-observer sensitivity
parts:
Adrian, it sounds like you need to examine your data and the fit of your=20
models. You record observations by 50m bin, but it sounds like most of=20
your observations fall in the first bin, which will make them impossible=20
to model reliably. Possibly adding in data for the rarer species has=20
made this problem worse. This could happen for example if the rarer=20
species are less likely to be identified if they are beyond 50m, making=20
the apparent detection function very spiked. g(0)=3D1 means exactly what=
=20
it suggests - det prob at distance zero is one. It says nothing about=20
det prob in the interval 0-50m.

You need to look at why most of your data are in the first interval. It=20
could be that your birds are not very detectable beyond the first 50m -=20
which suggests you have a poor choice of distance intervals. However,=20
this seems unlikely for seabirds. It may be that many of your birds are=20
in flight. If you just record birds in flight at the position you first=20
detect them, this biases recorded distances towards zero - see the 2001=20
book (pp198-203) for discussion of this issue - and a suggested=20
solution. It may be that many of your birds are being attracted towards=20
the vessel, and aren't being detected prior to this responsive=20
movement. It may be that your observers are just estimating distances=20
visually without training - distances at sea are very difficult to=20
estimate, and it could be that birds well beyond 50m are being recorded=20
as if they're in the first interval.

The answer is likely to be in improving survey design and field=20
methods. e.g. binocular search rather than naked eye search, aids to=20
estimating distances, training of fieldworkers for distance estimation=20
and species ID, revision of choice of distance intervals, revised=20
protocol for flying birds, etc. You may not be able to extract anything=20
useful from existing data. If you do continue with the analysis of=20
existing data, you can try truncating data beyond say 200m or 250m, to=20
see if that helps. You will probably also need to over-ride the=20
automated model selection in Distance, and for example force Distance to=20
fit a half-normal detection function with no adjustments, to prevent it=20
fitting the spike in detections at zero distance. However, you can=20
expect your density estimates to be biased, especially if the spike in=20
the first distance interval is real, rather than due to measurement=20
error or bird movement.

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 76223116e105ddbc
messages.subject: Re: MRDS Single-observer sensitivity
parts:
You are correct that we have over twice as many detections in the first b=
in=20
as we do in any one of the other five bins. The species in question is th=
e=20
Short-tailed Shearwater, which was nearly always seen on the wing. We wer=
e=20
using the "snapshot" method of counting (and assigning distances) to all =
flying=20
birds once per 300m (following Gould and Forsell 1989). In your opinion, =
do you=20
believe waiting until they are abeam of the observer does a better job of=
=20
handling the bias?

I think our distance estimations are pretty good. We use 10x reticle bino=
culars=20
with very fine scale reticles that improved our estimation over visual es=
timates=20
quite a bit in field trials prior to the surveys. The biggest problem we =
had on=20
those cruises was our observation location. We were confined to the port =
side=20
of the bridge and we had a blind spot @ 40-60 deg of the viewing arc, whi=
ch=20
means that most detections were made through the front window. This=20
definitely constrained the perpendicular distances.=20

A secondary problem is that the observer that had the most detections of=20=

Short-tailed Shearwaters also had the most skewed distance distribution, =
with=20
65% of his observations in the first bin. Yikes! That sure does fit your =
list of=20
trouble.

The good news is that we conducted the same surveys again in 2009 from a=20=

different ship. We had much better visibility from our spot on the bridge=
and=20
that is reflected in much prettier detection distributions (wide shoulder=
s and a=20
chubbier tail in the last 2 bins) for the 2009 data, which I am analyzing=
=20
separately. I used the 2008 data as examples when conducting our training=
for=20
the 2009 field crew and I think it was a big eye-opener for everyone invo=
lved.
